Thread
THRED
noun
From the Saxon thraed, from thrawan, “to twist” — fibres twisted together into a single line; the smallest unit of every woven thing, and the least valuable object a man could name.

Biblical Definition

A thread is a twisted line of fibre — the smallest thing on the loom, and in Scripture the standing measure of what is negligible. Abram swears to the king of Sodom that he will not take so much as a thread or a shoelatchet from him, lest the king should say he had made Abram rich (Gen 14:23): the least thread of Sodom’s wealth was too much for a man whose portion was God. Samson snapped new ropes from off his arms “like a thread” (Jdg 16:12), the strongest cord reckoned as nothing to the Spirit’s strength. The Song praises a bride whose lips are “like a thread of scarlet” (Son 4:3), fine and vivid together. But the great thread of the Bible hangs in a window in Jericho. The spies charge Rahab: “thou shalt bind this line of scarlet thread in the window which thou didst let us down by” (Jos 2:18), and every soul she gathers under that roof lives while the city falls. She bound it at once, before the armies came, while the walls still stood and there was nothing to see (Jos 2:21). The thread saved nobody by its strength. It saved by being the appointed sign, the same red mark as the blood on the doorposts — a token of covenant, hung in faith, honoured by God.

Webster 1828 Definition

A small line of twisted fibre; hence the least or slenderest thing; in Scripture the scarlet token of Rahab’s deliverance.

expand to see more

THREAD, n. [Sax. thraed, from thrawan, to twist.] A small line of fibres twisted together, of flax, wool, cotton, or silk, used in sewing and weaving.

Hence, any thing very slender or of small value: “from a thread even to a shoelatchet” (Gen 14:23).

Figuratively, the continuous course of a discourse or narration — the thread of an argument.

In Jos 2:18 the scarlet thread bound in Rahab’s window, the token of her house’s preservation.

A threefold cord, of threads twisted together, is not quickly broken (Ecc 4:12).

Key Scripture

Jos 2:18 — "Behold, when we come into the land, thou shalt bind this line of scarlet thread in the window which thou didst let us down by: and thou shalt bring thy father, and thy mother, and thy brethren, and all thy father's household, home unto thee."

Jos 2:21 — "And she said, According unto your words, so be it. And she sent them away, and they departed: and she bound the scarlet line in the window."

Jdg 16:12 — "Delilah therefore took new ropes, and bound him therewith, and said unto him, The Philistines be upon thee, Samson. And there were liers in wait abiding in the chamber. And he brake them from off his arms like a thread."

Son 4:3 — "Thy lips are like a thread of scarlet, and thy speech is comely: thy temples are like a piece of a pomegranate within thy locks."

Modern Corruption

No modern movement contests the meaning of a thread; the loss is that Rahab’s scarlet line is read as a charming detail of a spy story rather than as the appointed token of covenant deliverance.

expand to see more

Rahab’s thread has suffered nothing worse than being made picturesque. Retold as adventure, the scarlet line becomes a clever signal — a marker so the soldiers would know which house to spare — and the whole weight of it drains away into logistics. But Scripture will not let it stay small. Rahab is named twice in the New Testament, once among the heroes of faith and once among those justified by works that proved faith real, and the God who reckoned her righteous set her in the line of David and of Christ Himself. The thread was not signage; it was the visible pledge of a sworn covenant, bound in the window by faith before there was any army in sight, and it is joined by every instinct of the type to the blood struck on the lintel in Egypt, where again a red mark on the outside of a house was the whole difference between the living and the dead.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the strength of a token is never in the token. A thread stops no soldier. A smear of lamb’s blood stops no destroyer. What saved Rahab’s household was the word of the men who swore to her and the God who stood behind their oath, and the thread was simply the appointed way of taking Him at His word. So it is with every sign God has given. Baptism does not wash the conscience and the Supper does not feed the soul by any power resident in water or bread; they are covenant tokens, and their whole value lies in the faithfulness of Him who appointed them. Bind the thread early, as Rahab did — while the walls still stand and nothing has begun to shake — and gather your household inside the house where the sign is hung.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The least thing on the loom — Abram’s measure of what he would not take, and Rahab’s scarlet token of deliverance.

expand to see more

Thread — Saxon thraed, from thrawan, to twist.

Hebrew chut, a line or thread (Jos 2:18; Ecc 4:12); tiqvah, a cord, in Jos 2:18’s “line.”

The proverbial name for the negligible: not a thread nor a shoelatchet (Gen 14:23).

Rahab’s scarlet thread joins the blood of the lintel (Exo 12:13) as a red token of covenant deliverance.

Son 4:3 uses it for fineness and vivid colour together in the praise of the bride.

Usage

"Abram would not take a thread of Sodom’s wealth — a man whose portion is God can afford to refuse."

"Rahab bound the line while the walls still stood: faith hangs the token before the shaking begins."

"The thread had no strength; the oath behind it had all the strength — which is how every covenant sign works."
